explanations.answer: There is no one like the LORD in all the earth
explanations.explanation: That's the whole point, baker. The LORD says it plainly: "…so you may know that there is no one like Me in all the earth." (Exodus 9:14) The plagues are not just trouble for Egypt. They are showing Pharaoh, king of Egypt, who the LORD is.

explanations.answer: Israel is stronger than the army of Egypt
explanations.explanation: I can see why you'd go there, friend, because it sounds like a showdown. But the LORD never says a word about Israel's strength or Egypt's army in this verse. He says He will send all His plagues so Pharaoh may know that there is no one like Him in all the earth (Exodus 9:14). The spotlight stays on the LORD.

explanations.answer: Moses is the greatest prophet in the land
explanations.explanation: That one's not it, friend. The LORD's message in this verse isn't about Moses at all. It's about Pharaoh knowing that "…there is no one like Me in all the earth." (Exodus 9:14) Moses is the one the LORD sends to deliver the message.

Power it is, baker. The LORD says, "But I have raised you up for this very purpose, that I might display My power to you, and that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth." (Exodus 9:16) Pharaoh is about to see it up close.

Wealth? Baker, I'm standing on a gold base and even I wouldn't say that's the point. The LORD says He raised Pharaoh up "…that I might display My power to you…" (Exodus 9:16). Power is the word, and it's not about money. Pharaoh is about to see exactly what that power looks like.

Laws, friend? That would be like me walking into my bakery and handing out a rulebook instead of cookies. Not this verse. The LORD says He raised Pharaoh up "…that I might display My power to you…" (Exodus 9:16). Laws never come up, and power does.
I wish that were the case, baker, but it isn't. The LORD says the opposite: "Still, you lord it over My people and do not allow them to go." (Exodus 9:17) Pharaoh is still holding on.
Right on the money, friend. The LORD tells Pharaoh, "Still, you lord it over My people and do not allow them to go." (Exodus 9:17) That word "still" says Pharaoh hasn't budged.

explanations.answer: Shelter the livestock and everything in the field
explanations.explanation: That's the order, baker. The LORD says, "So give orders now to shelter your livestock and everything you have in the field." (Exodus 9:19) Pharaoh gets a plan along with the warning.

explanations.answer: Drive the livestock away into the wilderness
explanations.explanation: Running them off sounds like a plan, but it's not the one the LORD gives. The order is to shelter the livestock and everything in the field (Exodus 9:19). Shelter means bring it in, friend, not send it out.

explanations.answer: Gather the people at the palace gates
explanations.explanation: The palace gates never come up, baker. The LORD's order is about the livestock and everything in the field: shelter them (Exodus 9:19). A crowd at the gates would have been a lot of people standing outside, and I don't think that helps.

True, and the LORD says it straight. "Every man or beast that remains in the field and is not brought inside will die when the hail comes down upon them." (Exodus 9:19) It's a heavy line, baker. The warning comes before the hail, and it begins with the LORD telling Pharaoh to give orders now to shelter his livestock and everything in the field.

This one is true, friend, and it's a heavy line. The LORD says, "Every man or beast that remains in the field and is not brought inside will die when the hail comes down upon them." (Exodus 9:19) The warning comes before the hail for a reason.

explanations.answer: Whether they feared the word of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's exactly what the text says, baker. Some officials "…feared the word of the LORD…" and hurried to shelter their servants and livestock, while "…those who disregarded the word of the LORD…" left them in the field (Exodus 9:20-21). Same warning, two responses.

explanations.answer: Whether they lived close to the palace
explanations.explanation: Distance never comes up, friend. The text sorts the officials by one thing only. Those who feared the word of the LORD hurried to bring their servants and livestock to shelter, and those who disregarded it left them in the field (Exodus 9:20-21). The difference was how they treated the LORD's word.

explanations.answer: Whether Moses had warned them himself
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say Moses spoke to any of these officials one by one, baker. It says the difference was the word of the LORD: some feared it and some disregarded it (Exodus 9:20-21). The warning was out there for all of them.

Thunder and lightning, baker! The sky went full drum solo with a light show on top. The text says, "The hail fell and the lightning continued flashing through it." (Exodus 9:24) Moses only stretched out his staff toward heaven, and the LORD sent the rest.

Wind and darkness, friend? Not this time. This sky was loud and flashing, nobody was sitting around in the dark. The text says the LORD sent "…thunder and hail, and lightning struck the earth." (Exodus 9:23) Thunder and lightning are what came with the hail.
Hold your horses, baker. Those are bugs, and this storm isn't about bugs. The hail came with thunder, and "…lightning struck the earth." (Exodus 9:23)
I get the guess, baker, but the trees didn't get away. The hail "…beat down every plant of the field and stripped every tree." (Exodus 9:25) Plants and trees both took it.
Good catch, friend. The text says the hail "…beat down every plant of the field and stripped every tree." (Exodus 9:25) The trees took the hit with everything else.

Goshen is right, baker. "The only place where it did not hail was in the land of Goshen, where the Israelites lived." (Exodus 9:26) The hail struck down everything in the field throughout the land of Egypt (Exodus 9:25). Goshen was the one place it did not touch.

Canaan is a real place, baker, but this passage never mentions it. Egypt gets pounded, and the one spot the hail skipped is "…the land of Goshen, where the Israelites lived." (Exodus 9:26) Picture the whole country under that storm and one patch the hail just walks around. That patch is Goshen.

Midian is a fine name, friend, but you won't find it in this passage. Look at what the verse says: "The only place where it did not hail was in the land of Goshen, where the Israelites lived." (Exodus 9:26) Everywhere else in Egypt took it. Goshen was the one place the hail left alone.

That's what Pharaoh says, baker. "This time I have sinned…" he says, and then, "The LORD is righteous, and I and my people are wicked." (Exodus 9:27) Those are big words from him. The next verses show what he does after the storm.

Far away? Baker, I think that's the last thing Pharaoh is feeling with thunder rattling his whole country. He doesn't say it. He says, "The LORD is righteous, and I and my people are wicked." (Exodus 9:27) He calls the LORD righteous, and he calls himself and his people wicked.
Pharaoh goes the other way, baker. He says, "The LORD is righteous, and I and my people are wicked." (Exodus 9:27) He puts the blame on himself and his people.

Pharaoh asks for prayer, baker. "Pray to the LORD, for there has been enough of God’s thunder and hail." (Exodus 9:28) He wants the storm to end. He adds, "I will let you go…" and asks Moses and Aaron to speak to the LORD about it.
A sacrifice isn't what he asks for, friend. Pharaoh says, "Pray to the LORD, for there has been enough of God’s thunder and hail." (Exodus 9:28) It's a request for prayer.

Heal the livestock? Friend, that sounds like a reasonable ask after a storm like that, but it's not what Pharaoh says. He wants the sky to stop: "Pray to the LORD, for there has been enough of God’s thunder and hail." (Exodus 9:28) His request is for prayer. Moses answers that he will spread out his hands to the LORD (Exodus 9:29).
The LORD, baker. Moses says the thunder will cease and the hail will stop "…so that you may know that the earth is the LORD’s." (Exodus 9:29) The whole earth, not just Goshen.

Close in the neighborhood, friend, but not the answer. Moses says the earth is "the LORD's." (Exodus 9:29) The LORD is called "…the God of the Hebrews…" earlier (Exodus 9:13), but the earth belongs to Him.

Not the Egyptians, baker, even with all that hail landing on their land. Moses says the thunder will cease and the hail will stop "…so that you may know that the earth is the LORD’s." (Exodus 9:29) He says the whole earth belongs to the LORD. Pharaoh is the one who needs to know it.

I wish it went that way, baker, but Moses says the opposite. "But as for you and your officials, I know that you still do not fear the LORD our God." (Exodus 9:30) That word "still" matters. Pharaoh had just said he had sinned, and Moses says this right after.

Right, friend. Moses tells Pharaoh, "But as for you and your officials, I know that you still do not fear the LORD our God." (Exodus 9:30) Pharaoh had just said, "The LORD is righteous…" yet Moses says they still do not fear the LORD. The word "still" is the key.

True, baker. The text says "…the wheat and spelt were not destroyed, because they are late crops." (Exodus 9:32) The barley was ripe and the flax was in bloom, so those were destroyed (Exodus 9:31). The crop's timing made the difference.
This one is true, friend. The wheat and spelt "…were not destroyed, because they are late crops." (Exodus 9:32) Some of the crops came through.

explanations.answer: He sins again and hardens his heart
explanations.explanation: That's what happens, baker. "When Pharaoh saw that the rain and hail and thunder had ceased, he sinned again and hardened his heart…" (Exodus 9:34) Only a few verses earlier he had said, "I will let you go…" (Exodus 9:28). The storm ended and so did his promise.

explanations.answer: He lets the Israelites go at once
explanations.explanation: I wish, friend. He had said, "I will let you go…" (Exodus 9:28) But once the storm ended, he "…sinned again and hardened his heart…" (Exodus 9:34)

explanations.answer: He sends Moses a gift of thanks
explanations.explanation: There's no gift in the text, baker. When Pharaoh saw that the storm had stopped, he "…sinned again and hardened his heart…" (Exodus 9:34) Thanks never shows up.

True, baker. The text says Pharaoh "…sinned again and hardened his heart—he and his officials." (Exodus 9:34) The officials joined him. The passage then says Pharaoh's heart was hardened and he would not let the Israelites go (Exodus 9:35).
Look at the end of the verse, friend. Pharaoh "…sinned again and hardened his heart—he and his officials." (Exodus 9:34) So the officials hardened their hearts right along with him.
